title: Steer by the teaching
hookLine: Arjuna asks to be taught; the Gita says steer by scripture, not desire
carry: let the teaching, not desire, be your measure
last: THE THREE GATES — DESIRE, ANGER, GREED.

cards: Go back to chapter two. Arjuna is sitting in his chariot, refusing to fight, sure of what he feels and sure of nothing else. Then he says something brave: my mind is confused about my duty.
I am your student. Teach me. That's where the whole Gita starts: not with Arjuna following his feelings, and not with blind obedience, but with a student asking for a chart.
Chapter sixteen closes the loop: steer by the wind of whatever you want right now, or by a chart people before you drew.

teach.b: Verse twenty-two picks up yesterday's three gates. Whoever is free of those three doors of darkness does what is good for their own self, and goes to the highest.
Verse twenty-three: whoever throws aside the rule of scripture and acts on the pull of desire reaches neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.
And verse twenty-four, the chapter's last word: so let scripture be your measure in deciding what to do and what not to do. Know what the rule says, and act in this world.
The word is shastra: teaching, a rule, a manual, sometimes a whole science. There are shastras for grammar, music, and how to live. Here the contrast isn't scripture against thinking.
It's scripture against kama, desire, the first of yesterday's gates.
Desire is a poor compass; it points to itself. Hindus read this verse in more than one way. For some, the shastra is the Vedas and the texts that follow them, learned from a teacher.
Others stress that the Gita itself is a shastra, and that knowing the rule means understanding its purpose, not just its letter.

That's why, in Hindu families, big choices, a wedding date, a child's name, a vow, are often taken to a guru, a priest or an elder who knows the texts: not to switch off thinking, but to borrow a chart older than your wants.
Chapter seventeen opens with Arjuna asking: what about people who don't follow the scripture's rules, but who worship with real faith? The Gita takes it up in the very next verse.

how: Some Hindus look to shastra, the Vedas and the texts that follow them as taught by a guru or family tradition, for guidance on ritual and conduct; Gita 16.24 is quoted for scripture as the measure of right action.

o: a teaching or rule to steer your choices by
a holy chant repeated to quiet the mind
a priest's blessing spoken over a home

games.q: steering by the chart — tap the pairs.

s: it sets scripture against desire, kama, the first of the three gates.
shastra can mean a rule, a manual or a whole science
there are shastras for grammar, music, architecture, and how to live.
chapter 17 opens by asking about people with faith who don't follow the rules

games.q: you're choosing what to do, and desire is pulling hard one way. what does Gita 16.24 say to steer by?
o: whatever you want most right now.
games.why: scripture as the measure. verse 23 says acting on desire alone misses perfection, happiness and the highest goal.

practice: Think of one decision on your mind, and let desire speak first: what do I want, right this minute? Then ask what the best teaching you know would say, a verse, a grandparent's rule, something from these two hundred days.
If you pray, ask, as Arjuna did, to be taught. Hold both answers side by side without choosing yet, and just see the difference.

wordCard.voice: Shastra, teaching, rule, authoritative text. Gita sixteen, twenty-four: let it be your measure for what to do and not do, rather than the pull of desire.

orig.note: Sanskrit: shastra, teaching, rule, authoritative text; in Gita 16.24, the measure of what to do.
